query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ synchrotron-based high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) combined with appropriate spectroscopic techniques will provide real-time, simultaneous monitoring of oxidation kinetics and phase evolution in high-temperature oxidizing environments, offering more accurate insight into both oxidation behavior and phase stability than conventional ex‐situ methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy, such as CrMnFeCoNi, in its homogenized, as-cast state with a predominantly FCC solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to controlled high-temperature oxidizing conditions (e.g., temperatures above 800 °C) while measuring in situ.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (e.g., 800–1300 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere with real-time synchrotron XRD and complementary spectroscopy.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase formation and transformation dynamics during oxidation, including transient oxide phases and possible decomposition of the single-phase structure.
generation.mechanism: The in situ method captures time–temperature-dependent changes by continuously monitoring the diffraction patterns and spectroscopic signals, thereby revealing both the kinetics of oxide scale formation and the onset or progression of phase transformations.
generation.predicted_outcome: Detection of transient oxidation stages and phase transition events during heat treatment that correlate with changes in the oxidation kinetics and phase stability, which remain unresolved in post-mortem ex situ analysis.
generation.baseline: Conventional ex situ methods such as post-mortem XRD and microscopy that only provide snapshots after cooling, missing dynamic evolution.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the method is constrained by the available instrumentation (e.g., synchrotron beam flux and detector resolution) and the ability to maintain a stable, high-temperature oxidizing environment; also, extremely rapid kinetics may challenge temporal resolution.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is expected to capture dynamic changes more effectively, uncertainties remain regarding the detection limits for extremely transient phases and potential interference from rapid oxidation reactions at very high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a CrMnFeCoNi alloy sample in a high-temperature oxidation cell and conduct in situ synchrotron-based XRD measurements combined with simultaneous spectroscopic analysis during controlled heating in an oxidizing atmosphere. Parallel experiments using conventional ex situ analysis (post-mortem XRD and SEM) should be performed on samples subjected to identical thermal profiles.
measurements: Real-time phase fraction data from in situ XRD
Oxide formation and evolution from in situ spectroscopy
Comparison of oxidation kinetics and phase changes between in situ and ex situ techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ technique does not reveal additional or earlier stage oxidation or phase transformation events compared to the conventional ex situ methods – or if the dynamic data does not lead to a more refined understanding of oxidation kinetics (i.e., the results are statistically indistinguishable) – then the hypothesis that this combined method provides superior and more detailed insight will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
